episodes.title: Two green tests
episodes.decision: a plausible patch that passes its two existing tests can still break the contract. A test derived from the contract (not from the patch) can expose the omitted rule. The same habit runs through the rest of the week: a generated program is not an executed one, context is not retraining, each event in an agent's trace establishes only its own thing, and a repaired helper can still leave its caller wrong.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,515
A developer opens a build dashboard.

2
00:00:02,515 --> 00:00:06,287
The build service reports "OK", with spaces around it.

3
00:00:06,287 --> 00:00:08,382
The dashboard shows "unknown".

4
00:00:08,717 --> 00:00:13,019
Someone proposes a patch, and both of its existing tests pass.

5
00:00:13,019 --> 00:00:14,615
So, is the patch right?

6
00:00:14,950 --> 00:00:18,414
By the end of this video, you'll derive one more test,

7
00:00:18,414 --> 00:00:23,739
from the contract instead of the patch, and see why two green tests weren't enough.

8
00:00:24,783 --> 00:00:27,232
Start with the contract, not the code.

9
00:00:27,232 --> 00:00:29,230
The status arrives as a string.

10
00:00:29,567 --> 00:00:32,962
Ignore surrounding whitespace and letter case.

11
00:00:32,962 --> 00:00:34,290
"OK" means passed.

12
00:00:34,290 --> 00:00:35,766
"Fail" means failed.

13
00:00:35,766 --> 00:00:39,900
Anything else, including an empty string, means unknown.

14
00:00:40,233 --> 00:00:45,260
Each rule is something we can test, before we ever look at a patch.

15
00:00:46,299 --> 00:00:48,153
Here is the proposed patch.

16
00:00:48,153 --> 00:00:51,106
It lowercases the status, then looks it up.

17
00:00:51,106 --> 00:00:56,737
Unpadded "OK" becomes passed, "fail" becomes failed, and anything else is unknown.

18
00:00:57,083 --> 00:01:00,241
Two existing tests check "ok" and "fail".

19
00:01:00,241 --> 00:01:01,011
Both pass.

20
00:01:01,011 --> 00:01:03,399
Those are real, passing checks.

21
00:01:03,733 --> 00:01:05,856
But which rules do they exercise?

22
00:01:05,856 --> 00:01:09,201
Neither input has a space or a capital letter in it.

23
00:01:09,201 --> 00:01:11,581
The whitespace rule was never tested.

24
00:01:12,616 --> 00:01:14,975
So derive a test from the contract.

25
00:01:14,975 --> 00:01:17,740
The input is "OK", with spaces around it.

26
00:01:17,740 --> 00:01:22,055
The contract says the answer is passed, whatever the patch does.

27
00:01:22,399 --> 00:01:22,903
Run it.

28
00:01:22,903 --> 00:01:28,088
The patch lowercases the input, keeps the spaces, finds no matching key,

29
00:01:28,088 --> 00:01:29,528
and returns unknown.

30
00:01:29,528 --> 00:01:30,609
The test fails.

31
00:01:30,609 --> 00:01:32,697
The plausible patch is wrong.

32
00:01:33,032 --> 00:01:34,651
Not every new input helps.

33
00:01:34,651 --> 00:01:39,195
"Cancelled" returns unknown from the faulty patch and from a correct one.

34
00:01:39,195 --> 00:01:42,680
It exercises the fallback, but it can't tell them apart.

35
00:01:43,714 --> 00:01:48,916
The repair is one call: strip the surrounding whitespace before lowercasing.

36
00:01:49,264 --> 00:01:53,442
Now compare both versions on six cases taken from the contract.

37
00:01:53,442 --> 00:01:56,027
The first patch passes four of the six.

38
00:01:56,027 --> 00:01:57,751
The repair passes all six.

39
00:01:58,098 --> 00:02:02,525
Keep the two original tests, and keep the new ones as regressions.

40
00:02:02,525 --> 00:02:05,812
Six cases are observations about those behaviors,

41
00:02:05,812 --> 00:02:08,361
not a proof for every possible string.

42
00:02:09,397 --> 00:02:11,529
Why does this matter for agents?

43
00:02:11,529 --> 00:02:15,527
Suppose a model writes the patch, and also writes its tests.

44
00:02:15,864 --> 00:02:19,576
If both assume unpadded input, they agree with each other,

45
00:02:19,576 --> 00:02:21,368
and both miss the same rule.

46
00:02:21,368 --> 00:02:26,231
That's a possible shared omission, not a claim about how often models do it.

47
00:02:26,580 --> 00:02:31,760
Independent expected results come from somewhere else: the product contract,

48
00:02:31,760 --> 00:02:33,941
and cases you choose on purpose.

49
00:02:34,980 --> 00:02:37,800
Suppose a model had proposed this patch.

50
00:02:37,800 --> 00:02:39,492
How would it produce it?

51
00:02:39,492 --> 00:02:45,342
A language model processes tokens: word fragments, punctuation and code characters.

52
00:02:45,342 --> 00:02:50,911
At each step, it computes a distribution for the next token, given the context,

53
00:02:50,911 --> 00:02:52,039
and selects one.

54
00:02:52,039 --> 00:02:55,634
That token joins the context, and the step repeats.

55
00:02:55,980 --> 00:02:59,127
This can produce a useful multi-step algorithm.

56
00:02:59,127 --> 00:03:02,007
It does not mean the model has executed it.

57
00:03:02,007 --> 00:03:07,230
Valid Python can still implement a different rule from the one the user needs.

58
00:03:07,580 --> 00:03:13,503
And a token's likelihood is not a probability that the program satisfies the specification.

59
00:03:13,503 --> 00:03:18,644
The patch's behavior stays unobserved until an appropriate check actually runs.

60
00:03:19,680 --> 00:03:24,697
During ordinary inference, the workflow supplies a request and other context.

61
00:03:24,697 --> 00:03:30,496
Pasting a file or correcting an answer does not ordinarily update the model's parameters.

62
00:03:30,496 --> 00:03:32,841
Training changes learned parameters.

63
00:03:32,841 --> 00:03:36,816
Prompting changes what is available for the current response.

64
00:03:37,163 --> 00:03:38,909
Imagine two context packets.

65
00:03:38,909 --> 00:03:42,276
One holds only "fix the label" and the implementation.

66
00:03:42,276 --> 00:03:46,704
The other also holds "ignore surrounding whitespace" from the contract.

67
00:03:46,704 --> 00:03:49,385
The second supplies an explicit constraint.

68
00:03:49,385 --> 00:03:53,127
That does not mean the model will certainly succeed with it.

69
00:03:53,463 --> 00:03:55,394
Training is a different matter.

70
00:03:55,394 --> 00:04:00,438
Pretraining, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning change parameters,

71
00:04:00,438 --> 00:04:02,369
and can improve coding ability.

72
00:04:02,369 --> 00:04:04,237
They still leave requirements,

73
00:04:04,237 --> 00:04:07,662
versions and execution conditions to check at use time.

74
00:04:08,696 --> 00:04:12,543
A coding agent combines a model with an execution workflow.

75
00:04:12,543 --> 00:04:14,434
The model proposes an action.

76
00:04:14,434 --> 00:04:19,063
The controller checks the tool name, arguments, permissions and budget.

77
00:04:19,063 --> 00:04:23,627
And an allowed tool performs the operation and returns an observation.

78
00:04:23,963 --> 00:04:26,724
Each event establishes something different.

79
00:04:26,724 --> 00:04:29,613
An allowed read passed a permission decision.

80
00:04:29,613 --> 00:04:31,604
A write means a write occurred.

81
00:04:31,604 --> 00:04:35,585
And a model saying the work is finished is a completion claim.

82
00:04:35,930 --> 00:04:39,410
A permission decision does not establish correctness,

83
00:04:39,410 --> 00:04:42,036
and a write result is not a test result.

84
00:04:42,036 --> 00:04:45,057
If a test request is denied or never finishes,

85
00:04:45,057 --> 00:04:49,850
a later "all tests passed" message cannot supply the missing observation.

86
00:04:49,850 --> 00:04:54,118
A safe next step is to inspect the refusal or the missing result,

87
00:04:54,118 --> 00:04:55,760
and get an allowed check.

88
00:04:56,096 --> 00:05:00,931
Today's loop has one model, one controller decision and one tool result.

89
00:05:00,931 --> 00:05:05,229
A production coding agent wraps the same loop in more machinery:

90
00:05:05,229 --> 00:05:09,661
tool definitions and budgets, a compacted record of earlier steps,

91
00:05:09,661 --> 00:05:12,750
context files and skills, hooks and a sandbox,

92
00:05:12,750 --> 00:05:15,369
and a specification with a staged plan.

93
00:05:15,369 --> 00:05:18,726
Weeks two to four take these layers one at a time.

94
00:05:18,726 --> 00:05:23,091
Each layer changes what the model sees, or what an action may do.

95
00:05:23,091 --> 00:05:25,710
None of them checks the result for you.

96
00:05:25,710 --> 00:05:30,276
A richer harness still needs a completed check on the current files.

97
00:05:31,312 --> 00:05:32,725
Now look one level up.

98
00:05:32,725 --> 00:05:37,092
The developer also needs a failed-build count that matches the rows.

99
00:05:37,092 --> 00:05:39,853
The caller labels each row with the helper,

100
00:05:39,853 --> 00:05:43,770
but it counts failures by comparing the raw status to "fail".

101
00:05:44,112 --> 00:05:47,364
So repairing only the helper leaves a disagreement.

102
00:05:47,364 --> 00:05:52,592
For a padded, mixed-case failure, the row says failed, while the count stays zero.

103
00:05:52,592 --> 00:05:55,142
Even all six helper tests would miss it.

104
00:05:55,479 --> 00:05:58,867
The proposed repair counts the labels already computed.

105
00:05:58,867 --> 00:06:01,763
A full-output regression then checks the count,

106
00:06:01,763 --> 00:06:04,104
and the unchanged IDs and their order.

107
00:06:04,104 --> 00:06:07,553
These are hand-derived expectations, not a recorded run.

108
00:06:07,553 --> 00:06:08,786
And notice the task:

109
00:06:08,786 --> 00:06:13,591
"make tests pass" alone would not have said which product behavior to protect.

110
00:06:14,629 --> 00:06:16,393
So, back to the dashboard.

111
00:06:16,393 --> 00:06:19,719
Two green tests did not show the patch was right.

112
00:06:19,719 --> 00:06:23,452
One test derived from the contract showed it was wrong.

113
00:06:23,795 --> 00:06:25,032
One question to try.

114
00:06:25,032 --> 00:06:29,299
A new service sends "completed", and our contract maps it to unknown.

115
00:06:29,299 --> 00:06:30,660
Should it mean passed?

116
00:06:30,660 --> 00:06:35,545
Before you change anything, write the question you would ask the product owner.

episodes.title: Done is a claim
episodes.decision: an agent record that says read, write, then "done" with no further calls does not show that the bug is fixed. Report verified only when a passing check appears after the last write; the stop reason (`final` or `step_limit`) is reported separately, and a summary of the run is a claim too: it must keep the last failed check and be checked against the transcript (`notes:56-68`, `:221-228`).

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,851
Here is the complete record of an AI agent repairing a bug.

2
00:00:03,851 --> 00:00:04,830
It read a file.

3
00:00:04,830 --> 00:00:05,874
It wrote a file.

4
00:00:05,874 --> 00:00:09,137
Then it replied: done, and asked for nothing more.

5
00:00:09,483 --> 00:00:11,132
So, is the bug fixed?

6
00:00:11,467 --> 00:00:13,576
Nothing in this record can tell us.

7
00:00:13,576 --> 00:00:17,552
By the end of this video, you'll see which observation is missing,

8
00:00:17,552 --> 00:00:20,987
and why an agent saying "done" is a claim, not a verdict.

9
00:00:22,033 --> 00:00:25,945
First, let's separate two things we usually blur together.

10
00:00:26,283 --> 00:00:28,435
A language model produces text.

11
00:00:28,435 --> 00:00:29,755
That's all it does.

12
00:00:29,755 --> 00:00:35,518
Sometimes that text is shaped like a request: call this tool, with these arguments.

13
00:00:35,518 --> 00:00:37,393
We'll call that a proposal.

14
00:00:37,733 --> 00:00:42,394
The program around the model, the controller, decides what happens next.

15
00:00:42,394 --> 00:00:46,731
It checks the call: a tool it knows, the argument names it expects,

16
00:00:46,731 --> 00:00:49,320
a path it allows, and text it can write.

17
00:00:49,320 --> 00:00:52,234
Only then does the proposal become an action.

18
00:00:52,583 --> 00:00:55,546
When a call fails those checks, nothing runs.

19
00:00:55,546 --> 00:00:59,365
The controller sends back a refusal as that call's result,

20
00:00:59,365 --> 00:01:01,933
and the model sees it on its next turn.

21
00:01:01,933 --> 00:01:06,608
The model can ask for anything; the controller decides what is allowed.

22
00:01:07,648 --> 00:01:12,263
Let's watch the loop on the smallest task we could think of.

23
00:01:12,263 --> 00:01:15,725
A file, result.txt, contains the number five.

24
00:01:15,725 --> 00:01:17,494
It should contain four.

25
00:01:17,832 --> 00:01:20,339
On turn one, the model calls read.

26
00:01:20,339 --> 00:01:24,984
The controller runs it, and sends back the actual result: five.

27
00:01:24,984 --> 00:01:28,966
Every later request carries it: the file, not a guess.

28
00:01:29,315 --> 00:01:31,578
On turn two, the call is: write four.

29
00:01:31,578 --> 00:01:35,004
The controller writes it, and the tool reports: written.

30
00:01:35,348 --> 00:01:36,494
Should we stop now?

31
00:01:36,494 --> 00:01:37,338
It's tempting.

32
00:01:37,338 --> 00:01:39,026
The file probably says four.

33
00:01:39,026 --> 00:01:42,101
But "written" only tells us a side effect happened.

34
00:01:42,101 --> 00:01:45,356
It doesn't tell us the result meets the specification.

35
00:01:45,698 --> 00:01:48,259
On turn three, the call is: verify.

36
00:01:48,259 --> 00:01:53,160
A fixed check compares the file to the spec, and reports: verified.

37
00:01:53,160 --> 00:01:57,111
That result, under the call's own ID, is the evidence.

38
00:01:57,448 --> 00:02:02,626
On turn four, the model asks for nothing more, so the loop stops with final.

39
00:02:02,626 --> 00:02:06,441
The model proposes, the controller decides, a tool acts,

40
00:02:06,441 --> 00:02:09,848
and the observation goes back for the next choice.

41
00:02:09,848 --> 00:02:12,437
That circle is the core of this agent.

42
00:02:13,480 --> 00:02:16,559
Now rewind, and let the model make a mistake.

43
00:02:16,559 --> 00:02:19,569
On turn two, it writes five instead of four.

44
00:02:19,569 --> 00:02:21,280
The write still succeeds.

45
00:02:21,280 --> 00:02:23,332
The tool still says "written".

46
00:02:23,332 --> 00:02:25,590
Only the check notices: it fails.

47
00:02:25,930 --> 00:02:30,795
Now the model replies with no calls: "Verified." The loop stops with final,

48
00:02:30,795 --> 00:02:32,158
as the contract says.

49
00:02:32,158 --> 00:02:36,244
But that reply cannot change the result under the check's call,

50
00:02:36,244 --> 00:02:38,968
however convincing its explanation sounds.

51
00:02:39,314 --> 00:02:41,388
A message can describe the result.

52
00:02:41,388 --> 00:02:43,036
Only the check observes it.

53
00:02:43,036 --> 00:02:47,429
So report verified only when a passing check comes after the last write.

54
00:02:48,462 --> 00:02:50,143
So how does this loop end?

55
00:02:50,143 --> 00:02:54,151
There are only two stop reasons, and neither one is the check.

56
00:02:54,496 --> 00:02:57,028
Final: a reply had no tool calls.

57
00:02:57,028 --> 00:03:01,171
Step limit: the turn budget, four by default, ran out.

58
00:03:01,171 --> 00:03:05,544
The contract has no repeat detector, so without a budget,

59
00:03:05,544 --> 00:03:09,380
a model that keeps asking could go around forever.

60
00:03:09,729 --> 00:03:14,755
The check is read separately, from the history: the newest verify result,

61
00:03:14,755 --> 00:03:17,715
or not run, if a later write made it stale.

62
00:03:17,715 --> 00:03:22,534
Here, the check failed, the model wrote again, and the budget ran out.

63
00:03:22,534 --> 00:03:24,186
Stop reason: step limit.

64
00:03:24,186 --> 00:03:25,219
Check: not run.

65
00:03:25,219 --> 00:03:28,317
And that failure must be kept in any summary.

66
00:03:28,662 --> 00:03:31,053
Final means the conversation stopped.

67
00:03:31,053 --> 00:03:32,991
Verified means a check passed.

68
00:03:32,991 --> 00:03:36,674
The two are independent: in the notes' budget experiment,

69
00:03:36,674 --> 00:03:40,873
a three-turn run stops at the step limit with its check verified.

70
00:03:40,873 --> 00:03:42,618
Keep those two words apart.

71
00:03:43,662 --> 00:03:45,463
Now look at the tools.

72
00:03:45,463 --> 00:03:47,673
Each has a narrow contract.

73
00:03:47,673 --> 00:03:49,883
Read takes only result.txt.

74
00:03:49,883 --> 00:03:55,040
Write takes at most thirty-two characters, only for result.txt.

75
00:03:55,040 --> 00:03:58,314
Bash runs only the fixed verify command.

76
00:03:58,662 --> 00:04:04,016
Any other tool, argument name, path or command is refused before any effect,

77
00:04:04,016 --> 00:04:07,538
and the refusal goes back under the call's own ID.

78
00:04:07,538 --> 00:04:13,104
In our run of the fixture's tool function, each of these six came back refused,

79
00:04:13,104 --> 00:04:15,288
and result.txt still held five.

80
00:04:15,629 --> 00:04:18,152
So the name bash does not grant a shell.

81
00:04:18,152 --> 00:04:21,305
The adapter runs the literal verification program,

82
00:04:21,305 --> 00:04:24,270
and never puts model text into a shell command.

83
00:04:24,270 --> 00:04:27,991
And this dispatcher only limits calls that pass through it:

84
00:04:27,991 --> 00:04:30,640
the launcher supplies the outer isolation.

85
00:04:31,678 --> 00:04:35,209
When a project publishes its agent's instructions,

86
00:04:35,209 --> 00:04:40,859
read them as an engineer reads a configuration file, not as guaranteed behavior.

87
00:04:40,859 --> 00:04:45,660
Sort every sentence into four bins: a role or goal, a tool contract,

88
00:04:45,660 --> 00:04:49,686
a stopping or escalation rule, and a request for caution.

89
00:04:50,028 --> 00:04:52,897
Then ask of each one: what enforces this?

90
00:04:52,897 --> 00:04:54,997
A schema, the tool's own code,

91
00:04:54,997 --> 00:04:59,405
or a sandbox or permission check outside the model can enforce.

92
00:04:59,405 --> 00:05:02,274
A sentence that begins "never" only asks.

93
00:05:02,274 --> 00:05:07,032
Our loop makes the same split: the checks before any effect enforce,

94
00:05:07,032 --> 00:05:10,671
while the contract text in the prompt only proposes.

95
00:05:11,012 --> 00:05:12,449
Two habits carry over.

96
00:05:12,449 --> 00:05:15,063
A tool definition is part of the prompt.

97
00:05:15,063 --> 00:05:19,834
And long instructions are not evidence of safety: count what is enforced,

98
00:05:19,834 --> 00:05:21,140
not what is written.

99
00:05:21,140 --> 00:05:25,845
And one more difference: your four-turn loop never compacts its history;

100
00:05:25,845 --> 00:05:27,544
a production agent has to.

101
00:05:28,577 --> 00:05:34,430
So far, every request has carried the whole history: the task, every reply,

102
00:05:34,430 --> 00:05:36,147
and every tool result.

103
00:05:36,494 --> 00:05:40,351
A context window caps how much one request can carry,

104
00:05:40,351 --> 00:05:43,627
and each turn sends every earlier byte again.

105
00:05:43,627 --> 00:05:46,756
Four turns over a one-line file fit easily.

106
00:05:46,756 --> 00:05:48,940
A repository repair would not.

107
00:05:49,277 --> 00:05:52,303
Three kinds of content take most of the room.

108
00:05:52,303 --> 00:05:56,809
Tool output, like file reads and test logs, is usually the largest,

109
00:05:56,809 --> 00:05:58,624
and goes out of date first.

110
00:05:58,624 --> 00:06:01,314
Failed attempts stay, with their errors.

111
00:06:01,314 --> 00:06:03,735
Repeated reads add a copy each time.

112
00:06:03,735 --> 00:06:08,039
And the instructions and tool definitions go with every request.

113
00:06:09,077 --> 00:06:12,109
Overflowing the window is the obvious failure.

114
00:06:12,109 --> 00:06:13,691
Three others come first.

115
00:06:13,691 --> 00:06:17,250
Here is a longer history, from this week's self-check.

116
00:06:17,593 --> 00:06:18,851
Stale observations.

117
00:06:18,851 --> 00:06:24,545
The first read of the status file stays in the history after the agent has changed it.

118
00:06:24,545 --> 00:06:28,915
Nothing marks it out of date, so a later step can act on old text.

119
00:06:28,915 --> 00:06:30,703
Contradictions are similar:

120
00:06:30,703 --> 00:06:34,741
a failed attempt and the decision that replaced it both stay.

121
00:06:35,077 --> 00:06:36,264
Buried instructions.

122
00:06:36,264 --> 00:06:40,480
"Do not edit the view file" arrived once, inside a file the agent read.

123
00:06:40,480 --> 00:06:43,329
It now sits under everything that came after it,

124
00:06:43,329 --> 00:06:47,604
and nothing in the loop makes the model give it weight many turns later.

125
00:06:47,943 --> 00:06:51,294
Now clear every older tool result to a short stub,

126
00:06:51,294 --> 00:06:53,572
and keep the agent's own messages.

127
00:06:53,572 --> 00:06:57,526
The failure survives, but only in the agent's own sentence.

128
00:06:57,526 --> 00:06:59,738
The view-file constraint is gone.

129
00:06:59,738 --> 00:07:03,222
And nothing in what's left shows that it is missing.

130
00:07:04,260 --> 00:07:07,981
Summarising replaces older turns with written text.

131
00:07:07,981 --> 00:07:13,014
A useful summary keeps six things: the task and its acceptance check;

132
00:07:13,014 --> 00:07:18,923
each constraint and decision, with its source; what was tried, and how it failed;

133
00:07:18,923 --> 00:07:24,322
open failures, with the file version the check ran on; the files involved,

134
00:07:24,322 --> 00:07:26,875
and their state; and the next step.

135
00:07:26,875 --> 00:07:31,544
It drops raw tool output, which the agent can read or run again.

136
00:07:31,893 --> 00:07:33,044
Now generate one.

137
00:07:33,044 --> 00:07:36,023
Here is a summary written from that history.

138
00:07:36,023 --> 00:07:38,256
It reads well, and it is a claim.

139
00:07:38,256 --> 00:07:42,792
It kept the task, the edited file, and a next step: fix the lookup.

140
00:07:42,792 --> 00:07:47,056
It dropped the constraint, and the attempt that already failed.

141
00:07:47,393 --> 00:07:50,445
So the next step repeats the strip-only edit.

142
00:07:50,445 --> 00:07:55,532
We ran that edit on scratch files, and the same check failed on "OK" again.

143
00:07:55,877 --> 00:07:58,382
Check a summary like any generated work.

144
00:07:58,382 --> 00:08:03,268
For each item it should keep, find the message in the transcript it came from.

145
00:08:03,268 --> 00:08:08,217
Two have no match: the constraint, from the notes file, and the failed attempt,

146
00:08:08,217 --> 00:08:09,908
with the version it ran on.

147
00:08:09,908 --> 00:08:12,351
Add them back, each tied to its source.

148
00:08:12,693 --> 00:08:15,305
Then rerun the same check on the next step.

149
00:08:15,305 --> 00:08:19,436
Our next edit strips and lowercases, and leaves the view file alone.

150
00:08:19,436 --> 00:08:20,468
The check passes.

151
00:08:20,468 --> 00:08:24,234
But the check alone would not have caught the lost constraint.

152
00:08:24,234 --> 00:08:26,057
The transcript comparison did.

153
00:08:27,093 --> 00:08:29,681
When should you compact, and when restart?

154
00:08:29,681 --> 00:08:34,116
Compact when the task continues and the newest raw results still matter.

155
00:08:34,116 --> 00:08:40,707
Restart with a fresh context and a written handoff when most of the history is stale or contradicts itself,

156
00:08:40,707 --> 00:08:45,820
when one phase of the work has ended, or when the agent keeps failing the same way.

157
00:08:46,160 --> 00:08:49,019
A handoff holds the same items as a summary,

158
00:08:49,019 --> 00:08:52,268
written so that a new session can act on it alone.

159
00:08:52,268 --> 00:08:56,946
After either one, reread the files the next edit touches before editing.

160
00:08:57,993 --> 00:09:02,254
So, back to where we started: read, write, done.

161
00:09:02,593 --> 00:09:06,684
The missing observation was a passing check after the last write.

162
00:09:06,684 --> 00:09:08,760
With it, you may report verified.

163
00:09:08,760 --> 00:09:13,228
Without it, "done" is just a claim, and so is a summary nobody checked.

164
00:09:13,577 --> 00:09:16,867
One question to try before you compare with a partner.

165
00:09:16,867 --> 00:09:20,705
An agent writes the status file, and the acceptance tests fail.

166
00:09:20,705 --> 00:09:23,812
It writes the file again, and the turn budget ends.

167
00:09:23,812 --> 00:09:25,335
The new file looks right.

168
00:09:25,335 --> 00:09:28,685
What stop reason and check status does the record show?

169
00:09:28,685 --> 00:09:30,208
What must a summary keep?

170
00:09:30,208 --> 00:09:33,315
Which observation would let you report it verified?

171
00:09:33,315 --> 00:09:36,483
Write your answer, and the next check you would run.

episodes.title: Change only the context
episodes.decision: an agent acts only on what reaches it, so the context is an intervention you can test (`notes:21-23`). Trace the request path first; then compare contexts on the same task by changing the context only, with the question, the model, a fresh call, one call each and the checker fixed. Predict before running, keep predictions apart from what was observed, and claim no more than one pair shows (`notes:73-84`, `:118-121`, `:607`). The same holds in the middle of a session: build the next request four ways from one long history, run the same check on each, and check a summary against the transcript as well as by the next check (`notes:182-255`).

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:05,874
A dashboard shows a build whose raw status is OK, with spaces around it, as unknown.

2
00:00:05,874 --> 00:00:11,539
The agreed rule ignores surrounding whitespace and case, so it should say passed,

3
00:00:11,539 --> 00:00:14,826
while an unfamiliar status should stay unknown.

4
00:00:15,167 --> 00:00:17,827
A reviewer suggests editing the template.

5
00:00:17,827 --> 00:00:20,551
But an agent acts only on what reaches it.

6
00:00:20,551 --> 00:00:25,871
So first find where the value goes wrong, and which file the agent should inspect.

7
00:00:26,916 --> 00:00:28,588
Trace the request path.

8
00:00:28,588 --> 00:00:32,004
The loader keeps the raw value, spaces and all.

9
00:00:32,004 --> 00:00:36,002
The status mapper lowercases it, but the spaces remain,

10
00:00:36,002 --> 00:00:39,200
so it misses the key ok and returns unknown.

11
00:00:39,550 --> 00:00:42,259
So the first disagreement is in the mapper.

12
00:00:42,259 --> 00:00:44,023
Inspect normalization there:

13
00:00:44,023 --> 00:00:48,559
removing the surrounding whitespace before the lookup repairs this case.

14
00:00:48,900 --> 00:00:55,188
Changing every unknown in the template to passed would also mislabel an unfamiliar status.

15
00:00:55,188 --> 00:00:56,446
Check both inputs.

16
00:00:57,482 --> 00:00:59,218
That path was a schematic.

17
00:00:59,218 --> 00:01:02,824
The course dashboard has a real one, the project list.

18
00:01:02,824 --> 00:01:05,495
The route selects the caller's projects.

19
00:01:05,495 --> 00:01:09,835
A helper rejects a visitor without a session, with a four-oh-one.

20
00:01:09,835 --> 00:01:13,841
And the template prints, No projects yet, for an empty list.

21
00:01:14,182 --> 00:01:19,436
The route names what happens; the other two files decide what a visitor sees.

22
00:01:19,436 --> 00:01:22,234
So a map of this path is a set of claims.

23
00:01:22,234 --> 00:01:26,942
Mark each arrow confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell, at your revision.

24
00:01:27,982 --> 00:01:31,445
Now ask a model one bounded question about that path:

25
00:01:31,445 --> 00:01:33,993
what does a signed-out visitor receive,

26
00:01:33,993 --> 00:01:39,024
what does a signed-in user with no projects see, and which file decides each?

27
00:01:39,024 --> 00:01:42,553
Null is allowed for anything the context doesn't show.

28
00:01:42,899 --> 00:01:47,971
Two packets carry the same number of bytes, six hundred and thirty-nine each.

29
00:01:47,971 --> 00:01:49,750
Only their content differs.

30
00:01:49,750 --> 00:01:52,846
Packet A reads on through the route's own file.

31
00:01:52,846 --> 00:01:58,380
Packet B follows the call across files: the four-oh-one line, the route, the helper,

32
00:01:58,380 --> 00:02:00,488
and the template's empty branch.

33
00:02:00,832 --> 00:02:03,610
Predict each packet's four answers first.

34
00:02:03,610 --> 00:02:09,031
Keep the model, the question, a fresh call, one call each and the checker fixed.

35
00:02:09,031 --> 00:02:12,825
Change the packet only, and don't rerun until it passes.

36
00:02:13,864 --> 00:02:19,425
The checker labels each field correct, wrong, abstained for an explicit null,

37
00:02:19,425 --> 00:02:23,180
or missing, using answers from the dashboard itself.

38
00:02:23,180 --> 00:02:27,296
An abstention is honest; a confident wrong file is worse.

39
00:02:27,630 --> 00:02:29,911
To show how it reads two answers,

40
00:02:29,911 --> 00:02:34,264
the course team wrote one plausible answer per packet, by hand.

41
00:02:34,264 --> 00:02:35,646
No model was called.

42
00:02:35,646 --> 00:02:38,824
Packet A's answer gets none of the four right.

43
00:02:38,824 --> 00:02:42,417
Packet B's gets three: the route passes the list on,

44
00:02:42,417 --> 00:02:44,767
but the template decides the text.

45
00:02:45,114 --> 00:02:49,682
That replay says nothing about how often a model answers either way;

46
00:02:49,682 --> 00:02:51,898
your own pair is the measurement.

47
00:02:51,898 --> 00:02:55,324
A tie, or A beating B, is a legitimate observation,

48
00:02:55,324 --> 00:02:59,557
and one pair motivates a next experiment, nothing more general.

49
00:03:00,596 --> 00:03:04,685
In this exercise we load the packet into the prompt ourselves:

50
00:03:04,685 --> 00:03:06,532
no filename acts on its own.

51
00:03:06,532 --> 00:03:11,281
A context file that exists but was never loaded cannot explain a result.

52
00:03:11,281 --> 00:03:14,052
So verify what actually reached the model.

53
00:03:14,396 --> 00:03:17,572
Then build a packet of your own for a second question,

54
00:03:17,572 --> 00:03:21,983
in at most four hundred bytes, each excerpt under a header naming its file.

55
00:03:21,983 --> 00:03:26,923
Its check says whether the evidence is in the packet, not what a model would answer.

56
00:03:27,961 --> 00:03:31,701
A summary is context you choose in the middle of a session,

57
00:03:31,701 --> 00:03:33,729
when the history no longer fits.

58
00:03:33,729 --> 00:03:39,053
The course wrote one long session by hand: an agent repairing this same status case,

59
00:03:39,053 --> 00:03:41,969
nineteen messages, just under its byte budget.

60
00:03:41,969 --> 00:03:44,250
The next check result would not fit.

61
00:03:44,595 --> 00:03:48,424
The compaction script builds the next request four ways.

62
00:03:48,424 --> 00:03:50,133
Full keeps every message.

63
00:03:50,133 --> 00:03:53,483
Auto keeps the task and the agent's own messages,

64
00:03:53,483 --> 00:03:57,106
and clears longer old tool results to one-line stubs.

65
00:03:57,106 --> 00:04:01,004
Summary puts your summary in place of the older messages.

66
00:04:01,004 --> 00:04:05,516
Fresh keeps only the task and your file: a restart from a handoff.

67
00:04:05,861 --> 00:04:08,700
Then a course-written policy, not a model,

68
00:04:08,700 --> 00:04:13,972
picks the next edit from that context alone, and the same six-case check runs.

69
00:04:13,972 --> 00:04:19,852
It keeps out of the view file only if a line names that file and says not to change it.

70
00:04:19,852 --> 00:04:23,636
Otherwise it makes the template patch we warned against.

71
00:04:24,677 --> 00:04:30,023
Predict first: which facts auto keeps, and which file the next edit touches.

72
00:04:30,023 --> 00:04:30,657
Then run.

73
00:04:30,657 --> 00:04:36,285
With the full history, the next edit strips and lowercases in the status mapper:

74
00:04:36,285 --> 00:04:37,410
six of six pass.

75
00:04:37,410 --> 00:04:42,968
With auto, it lands in the view file, and the check fails: queued shows passed,

76
00:04:42,968 --> 00:04:44,797
and the view file changed.

77
00:04:45,143 --> 00:04:50,281
The rule arrived once, in the middle of a tool result: the contributor notes,

78
00:04:50,281 --> 00:04:51,616
read in message two.

79
00:04:51,616 --> 00:04:54,018
Clearing old tool output removed it.

80
00:04:54,018 --> 00:04:57,954
Nothing left in the context contradicts the view-file edit,

81
00:04:57,954 --> 00:05:02,024
which is why this loss is hard to see from the context alone.

82
00:05:02,360 --> 00:05:05,520
Now generate a summary and run it the same way.

83
00:05:05,520 --> 00:05:10,965
In our run, one that says only, do not edit the template, fails just as auto did.

84
00:05:10,965 --> 00:05:15,469
One that names the view file, and where the rule came from, passes,

85
00:05:15,469 --> 00:05:17,485
as a summary and as a restart.

86
00:05:17,485 --> 00:05:19,972
It passes only if it keeps that rule.

87
00:05:20,310 --> 00:05:23,575
But a passing check is not the whole verification.

88
00:05:23,575 --> 00:05:27,690
Every mode keeps the task, and the policy reads only two facts.

89
00:05:27,690 --> 00:05:32,784
A summary can pass and still leave out which read of the status file is stale.

90
00:05:32,784 --> 00:05:35,984
So fill the checklist against the transcript too.

91
00:05:36,327 --> 00:05:39,505
Compact when the newest results still matter.

92
00:05:39,505 --> 00:05:44,025
Restart when most of the history is stale or contradicts itself,

93
00:05:44,025 --> 00:05:45,508
or a phase has ended.

94
00:05:45,508 --> 00:05:48,757
Either way, reread the files the edit touches.

95
00:05:48,757 --> 00:05:53,277
This comparison is Activity 5: optional practice, with no marks.

96
00:05:54,326 --> 00:05:59,920
A skill packages a procedure: a SKILL.md file with a name, a description and a body.

97
00:05:59,920 --> 00:06:03,582
An agent keeps only the names and descriptions in view,

98
00:06:03,582 --> 00:06:06,845
and loads a body when a request seems to need it.

99
00:06:06,845 --> 00:06:10,708
So the description decides whether the skill is ever used.

100
00:06:11,043 --> 00:06:14,736
A description that says only when can miss other phrasings;

101
00:06:14,736 --> 00:06:18,305
one that says only what can fire on every label question.

102
00:06:18,305 --> 00:06:22,938
So test the trigger: three requests in people's words that should load it,

103
00:06:22,938 --> 00:06:25,943
and one near miss, like rename the label column.

104
00:06:25,943 --> 00:06:27,947
Predict each before you observe.

105
00:06:28,293 --> 00:06:32,469
A near miss that fires means the description is too broad.

106
00:06:32,469 --> 00:06:35,998
A missed request usually shares no words with it.

107
00:06:35,998 --> 00:06:39,887
Neither a context file nor a skill grants permissions.

108
00:06:39,887 --> 00:06:44,208
Use yours once on the course dashboard, and once, read-only,

109
00:06:44,208 --> 00:06:46,080
on your candidate project.

110
00:06:46,080 --> 00:06:48,529
A skill nobody has run is a draft.

111
00:06:49,575 --> 00:06:51,142
Tools are context too.

112
00:06:51,142 --> 00:06:55,201
Through a protocol such as MCP, or a plain function call,

113
00:06:55,201 --> 00:06:59,616
the agent sees each tool's name, description and input schema,

114
00:06:59,616 --> 00:07:01,468
and reads results as data.

115
00:07:01,468 --> 00:07:06,595
It chooses from that text alone, so design for a reader that will guess.

116
00:07:06,942 --> 00:07:09,195
Five rules turn that into checks.

117
00:07:09,195 --> 00:07:11,244
Put every limit in the schema.

118
00:07:11,244 --> 00:07:13,771
Return only what the next step needs.

119
00:07:13,771 --> 00:07:17,049
Report a failure as a result the agent can read.

120
00:07:17,049 --> 00:07:20,668
Say what comes back, and where each input comes from.

121
00:07:20,668 --> 00:07:23,126
And guard every irreversible action.

122
00:07:23,475 --> 00:07:28,671
The notes' first draft of a search tool and a delete tool looks finished.

123
00:07:28,671 --> 00:07:31,944
But reading it is not verification; calls are.

124
00:07:31,944 --> 00:07:36,143
In our run, the draft returns names with no IDs to pass on.

125
00:07:36,143 --> 00:07:37,709
A bare delete deletes.

126
00:07:37,709 --> 00:07:40,485
An unknown ID crashes with a traceback.

127
00:07:40,485 --> 00:07:44,826
And a limit of fifty is accepted: it lives only in the prose.

128
00:07:45,175 --> 00:07:50,742
The revision returns label IDs, only previews a delete unless dry run is turned off,

129
00:07:50,742 --> 00:07:54,388
returns a not-found error that says a retry won't help,

130
00:07:54,388 --> 00:07:57,768
and rejects the out-of-range limit from its schema.

131
00:07:57,768 --> 00:08:00,021
Each row is a check you can rerun.

132
00:08:00,021 --> 00:08:03,600
A new rule needs a new call, not a longer description.

133
00:08:04,641 --> 00:08:09,314
Now give one request to an agent on each server: delete red-team,

134
00:08:09,314 --> 00:08:11,830
with a wrong ID from an old ticket.

135
00:08:11,830 --> 00:08:16,430
The replay agent is a fixed, course-written policy, not a model.

136
00:08:16,430 --> 00:08:20,600
On the draft, it hits a traceback, finds no ID, and stops.

137
00:08:20,600 --> 00:08:25,632
On the revision, it reads not found, searches, previews, then deletes.

138
00:08:25,974 --> 00:08:30,343
If the old ID belongs to another label, the draft deletes it at once.

139
00:08:30,343 --> 00:08:35,281
The revision only previews it, so the agent sees the wrong name, and searches.

140
00:08:35,281 --> 00:08:37,813
The brake didn't make the agent smarter;

141
00:08:37,813 --> 00:08:41,485
it turned a wrong call into a result the agent could read.

142
00:08:41,824 --> 00:08:44,926
Three layers keep a wrong call from doing harm.

143
00:08:44,926 --> 00:08:48,622
The brake makes a call that leaves out dry run harmless.

144
00:08:48,622 --> 00:08:51,922
A pre-call hook checks an event before its effect.

145
00:08:51,922 --> 00:08:56,740
Neither contains a process that edits or ignores them; the launcher does.

146
00:08:56,740 --> 00:09:00,040
A hook that logs afterwards has prevented nothing.

147
00:09:01,074 --> 00:09:03,594
So treat context as an intervention.

148
00:09:03,594 --> 00:09:06,255
Change one thing, keep the rest fixed,

149
00:09:06,255 --> 00:09:10,106
and keep your predictions apart from what you observed.

150
00:09:10,440 --> 00:09:11,737
One question to try.

151
00:09:11,737 --> 00:09:17,833
Packet B's answer gets every field right only after a second call that adds the template file.

152
00:09:17,833 --> 00:09:21,854
Can the difference from packet A be attributed to B's content?

153
00:09:21,854 --> 00:09:27,043
Write the expected behavior and the next check, before comparing with a partner.

episodes.title: Not passed is not failed
episodes.decision: a requirement has to be traced from an observed event, not invented in the request. Ask about a past event; keep observation, inference and what you cannot conclude apart; write the problem statement by hand and check each clause against the observation; write an acceptance criterion that labels its design choices; then judge a generated candidate against that criterion. The trace runs `S4-A → P1 → AC1 → AC1-mixed → predicate repair`, and a passing test cannot turn a design choice into user evidence. The same criterion is then handed to an agent in stages (research, propose, plan, implement, test), with a person's decision at every stop: a candidate is read against its bound before it is tested, a failed check means the later checks were not run, and a round that stops after Plan, as the course's worked round on `ci-dashboard` does, is a legitimate result.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:01,385
In a made-up scenario,

2
00:00:01,385 --> 00:00:06,168
a maintainer checks run results before choosing a failed job to investigate.

3
00:00:06,168 --> 00:00:10,008
A filter for runs that have not passed shows nine and eleven.

4
00:00:10,350 --> 00:00:11,633
They open run eleven.

5
00:00:11,633 --> 00:00:12,794
It's still running.

6
00:00:12,794 --> 00:00:14,504
So they go back to the list,

7
00:00:14,504 --> 00:00:18,047
and keep a handwritten list of the failed run IDs instead.

8
00:00:19,083 --> 00:00:22,041
Discovery starts with a past event, not a pitch.

9
00:00:22,041 --> 00:00:24,567
Not "would you use our smart dashboard?",

10
00:00:24,567 --> 00:00:27,895
but "walk me through the last time you checked a run."

11
00:00:28,233 --> 00:00:31,692
Then keep what you saw apart from what you infer.

12
00:00:31,692 --> 00:00:34,798
Observed: the filter included a running job.

13
00:00:34,798 --> 00:00:40,586
Inferred: mixing running and failed jobs may distract from investigating failures.

14
00:00:40,933 --> 00:00:44,324
And keep what you can't conclude yet: how common this is,

15
00:00:44,324 --> 00:00:47,655
or whether a separate filter is the preferred interface.

16
00:00:48,700 --> 00:00:54,106
Write the problem statement by hand: the maintainer cannot isolate failed runs,

17
00:00:54,106 --> 00:00:57,802
because the current filter also includes running runs.

18
00:00:58,150 --> 00:01:01,335
Then check each clause against the observation.

19
00:01:01,335 --> 00:01:03,843
"Everyone needs instant alerts" goes:

20
00:01:03,843 --> 00:01:07,774
neither "everyone" nor alerts has any supporting evidence.

21
00:01:08,816 --> 00:01:13,691
The small spec keeps the decisions: a pure function, failed IDs,

22
00:01:13,691 --> 00:01:16,357
from a list of ID and status pairs.

23
00:01:16,357 --> 00:01:20,775
Its non-goals include a web UI, notifications and retries.

24
00:01:21,116 --> 00:01:25,218
Ascending order is a design decision, not an interview finding,

25
00:01:25,218 --> 00:01:26,585
and the spec says so.

26
00:01:26,933 --> 00:01:30,410
The acceptance criterion: return the ascending,

27
00:01:30,410 --> 00:01:36,551
duplicate-free IDs whose status is exactly failed, an empty list if there are none,

28
00:01:36,551 --> 00:01:38,770
and leave the input unchanged.

29
00:01:38,770 --> 00:01:43,431
It replaces the ambiguous request, show jobs needing attention.

30
00:01:44,466 --> 00:01:45,508
Predict first.

31
00:01:45,508 --> 00:01:50,643
A plausible generated candidate keeps every status that isn't passed.

32
00:01:50,983 --> 00:01:54,319
On the observed runs it returns nine and eleven.

33
00:01:54,319 --> 00:01:56,682
The criterion requires nine alone.

34
00:01:56,682 --> 00:02:00,990
The problem is how "needs attention" was read, not the syntax.

35
00:02:02,032 --> 00:02:07,303
Repair the predicate to status equals failed, and run the same checks again.

36
00:02:07,649 --> 00:02:12,726
The public checks cover mixed statuses, empty input, no failures, sorting,

37
00:02:12,726 --> 00:02:17,049
duplicates and another ID, and the input has to stay unchanged.

38
00:02:17,049 --> 00:02:19,038
On the repair, they all pass.

39
00:02:20,082 --> 00:02:25,380
Trace the decision: the observation, the problem statement, the criterion,

40
00:02:25,380 --> 00:02:27,814
the failing check, and the repair.

41
00:02:28,149 --> 00:02:32,547
A passing test of the ordering rule doesn't turn it into interview evidence.

42
00:02:32,547 --> 00:02:35,962
And acceptance tests can't show that the product is useful.

43
00:02:36,998 --> 00:02:39,017
AC1 says what must be true.

44
00:02:39,017 --> 00:02:42,681
It does not say how to hand the work to an agent.

45
00:02:42,681 --> 00:02:47,841
One request, implement AC1, asks the agent to research, choose, plan,

46
00:02:47,841 --> 00:02:52,254
write and judge in a single step, and you only see the end.

47
00:02:52,598 --> 00:02:58,009
So split it into five stages: research, propose, plan, implement, and test.

48
00:02:58,009 --> 00:03:03,565
At every stop, a person reads what the stage produced, and decides: continue,

49
00:03:03,565 --> 00:03:07,389
narrow the task, return to an earlier stage, or stop.

50
00:03:07,731 --> 00:03:10,580
An agent can draft the output of every stage.

51
00:03:10,580 --> 00:03:13,048
It cannot make those decisions for you,

52
00:03:13,048 --> 00:03:16,276
and it cannot be the one who checks its own result.

53
00:03:17,314 --> 00:03:20,968
At propose, suppose the agent offers three options.

54
00:03:20,968 --> 00:03:24,623
A: change the predicate inside the broken function.

55
00:03:24,623 --> 00:03:30,283
It is the smallest diff, but it removes the counterexample the class relies on.

56
00:03:30,631 --> 00:03:35,542
B: add a separate failed-ids function, checked by the same verify.

57
00:03:35,542 --> 00:03:39,039
One new function, and the counterexample stays.

58
00:03:39,039 --> 00:03:42,461
C: add a status option to the run list screen.

59
00:03:42,461 --> 00:03:44,470
But a web UI is a non-goal.

60
00:03:44,814 --> 00:03:45,665
You choose B.

61
00:03:45,665 --> 00:03:49,789
Rejecting C is a scope decision from the requirements document,

62
00:03:49,789 --> 00:03:53,127
not a technical judgement, so write it down as one.

63
00:03:54,164 --> 00:04:00,116
At plan, each step points to a check written from AC1 before any code existed.

64
00:04:00,116 --> 00:04:05,153
Keep only status exactly failed: the mixed and no-failures checks.

65
00:04:05,153 --> 00:04:08,282
Return each ID once: the duplicate check.

66
00:04:08,631 --> 00:04:10,901
Sort ascending: the sort check.

67
00:04:10,901 --> 00:04:13,246
Handle no runs: the empty check.

68
00:04:13,246 --> 00:04:17,055
Use the input, not fixed values: the other-ID check.

69
00:04:17,055 --> 00:04:22,841
And do not change the input: the assertion that reports the input was modified.

70
00:04:23,181 --> 00:04:27,151
If a step has no check, write the check first, or drop the step.

71
00:04:27,151 --> 00:04:29,508
The plan is where you narrow the task.

72
00:04:30,547 --> 00:04:35,537
At implement, the bound is part of the request: write only failed-ids,

73
00:04:35,537 --> 00:04:40,670
in one new file, with no imports, and do not edit the acceptance checks.

74
00:04:40,670 --> 00:04:45,303
Without a model, the course wrote three candidates for this stop.

75
00:04:45,647 --> 00:04:50,233
Read each one as text, and decide whether it stays inside the bound,

76
00:04:50,233 --> 00:04:51,581
before it is tested.

77
00:04:51,581 --> 00:04:55,493
Anything outside the bound is rejected, even if it passes.

78
00:04:55,493 --> 00:05:00,213
In the activity, one candidate passes Test and still breaks the bound.

79
00:05:00,213 --> 00:05:02,911
Which one, and why didn't Test catch it?

80
00:05:02,911 --> 00:05:04,664
That one is yours to find.

81
00:05:05,014 --> 00:05:09,539
Then test, and record the exit code with the first failing check,

82
00:05:09,539 --> 00:05:11,279
or the one all-pass line.

83
00:05:11,279 --> 00:05:15,595
In our run of the broken version, the mixed check fails first,

84
00:05:15,595 --> 00:05:17,544
so the other five never run.

85
00:05:17,544 --> 00:05:22,626
After a failure, the later checks are not run, and not run is not passed.

86
00:05:23,664 --> 00:05:25,996
A failure tells you where to go back.

87
00:05:25,996 --> 00:05:30,281
A wrong predicate, like the one our run of the broken version shows,

88
00:05:30,281 --> 00:05:31,857
returns you to implement.

89
00:05:31,857 --> 00:05:35,134
A clause the plan never covered returns you to plan.

90
00:05:35,134 --> 00:05:38,727
A misread requirement returns you to propose or research.

91
00:05:38,727 --> 00:05:41,752
And never repair a failure by editing the check.

92
00:05:42,097 --> 00:05:47,090
Record the round in a few lines: the brief for each stage, what came back,

93
00:05:47,090 --> 00:05:49,181
and your decision at each stop.

94
00:05:49,181 --> 00:05:53,769
Stopping after plan, because the first step is not yet small enough,

95
00:05:53,769 --> 00:05:55,321
is a legitimate result.

96
00:05:56,364 --> 00:05:59,565
Between stages, each one hands the next a file.

97
00:05:59,565 --> 00:06:03,107
The research file holds the located claims you kept;

98
00:06:03,107 --> 00:06:06,104
the plan file holds the step-to-check table.

99
00:06:06,104 --> 00:06:12,235
The next stage starts in a fresh session that reads only that file and the paths it names,

100
00:06:12,235 --> 00:06:14,823
not the conversation that produced it.

101
00:06:14,823 --> 00:06:19,523
The course's research and plan skills return those claims and tables;

102
00:06:19,523 --> 00:06:20,954
the stops stay yours.

103
00:06:21,997 --> 00:06:25,326
Here is the same round on the project repository.

104
00:06:25,326 --> 00:06:28,994
The course wrote this record, and no model was called.

105
00:06:28,994 --> 00:06:29,945
The criterion:

106
00:06:29,945 --> 00:06:34,700
an owner's overview lists the active project and not the archived one,

107
00:06:34,700 --> 00:06:37,961
and the archived project's own page still opens.

108
00:06:38,297 --> 00:06:41,727
Research returns four claims, each with a location.

109
00:06:41,727 --> 00:06:42,736
Open every one.

110
00:06:42,736 --> 00:06:47,242
The fourth says the overview query already skips archived projects,

111
00:06:47,242 --> 00:06:49,528
so only the label needs to change.

112
00:06:49,528 --> 00:06:52,218
But the query has no archived condition.

113
00:06:52,218 --> 00:06:52,891
Strike it.

114
00:06:53,230 --> 00:06:57,106
Had it survived, the plan would have changed only the label,

115
00:06:57,106 --> 00:07:00,143
and the archived project would still be listed.

116
00:07:00,143 --> 00:07:03,114
A wrong research claim becomes a wrong option,

117
00:07:03,114 --> 00:07:05,569
then a wrong plan step and wrong code.

118
00:07:05,569 --> 00:07:09,833
Striking it at the first stop is the cheapest repair in the round.

119
00:07:10,180 --> 00:07:13,644
At propose, filter in the query, not in the template:

120
00:07:13,644 --> 00:07:16,584
for an owner whose projects are all archived,

121
00:07:16,584 --> 00:07:21,419
the template's empty branch would never run, and the table would be blank.

122
00:07:21,419 --> 00:07:25,471
The plan changes one line, and adds two tests, one per clause.

123
00:07:25,814 --> 00:07:29,986
Then writing the tests exposes a case the criterion never names:

124
00:07:29,986 --> 00:07:32,659
an owner whose projects are all archived.

125
00:07:32,659 --> 00:07:36,049
That owner reads "No projects yet", which is untrue,

126
00:07:36,049 --> 00:07:40,939
and gets back to the unarchive button only by typing the project's address.

127
00:07:40,939 --> 00:07:42,699
Neither is a code question.

128
00:07:42,699 --> 00:07:47,849
So the round stops after plan, and both questions go back to the specification.

129
00:07:48,896 --> 00:07:51,004
Treat specifications as source.

130
00:07:51,004 --> 00:07:55,628
Version the intent, and review its changes alongside tests and code.

131
00:07:55,628 --> 00:08:00,727
A requirement change should identify the affected tests and implementation,

132
00:08:00,727 --> 00:08:05,011
and a code change should still satisfy the current requirement.

133
00:08:05,011 --> 00:08:09,295
Record each agreed change in the spec's change log: the clause,

134
00:08:09,295 --> 00:08:12,627
the tests it affects, the reason, and who agreed.

135
00:08:12,963 --> 00:08:17,516
But prose is not automatically executable, complete or true.

136
00:08:17,516 --> 00:08:21,842
A mistaken spec can produce consistent but unwanted code.

137
00:08:21,842 --> 00:08:27,533
And an AI consistency report is a review input, not a proof of correctness.

138
00:08:28,579 --> 00:08:31,050
So start from an event, not a pitch.

139
00:08:31,050 --> 00:08:32,766
Label the design choices.

140
00:08:32,766 --> 00:08:36,266
And judge the generated code against the criterion,

141
00:08:36,266 --> 00:08:38,668
not against how plausible it looks.

142
00:08:39,013 --> 00:08:40,199
One question to try.

143
00:08:40,199 --> 00:08:42,394
The filter returns the right records,

144
00:08:42,394 --> 00:08:45,776
but sorts them differently from the agreed display order.

145
00:08:45,776 --> 00:08:47,496
Is the requirement satisfied?

146
00:08:47,496 --> 00:08:50,344
Write the expected behavior, and the next check.

episodes.title: Shorter, same contract
episodes.decision: a shorter refactor still has to keep the behavior callers rely on. First freeze that behavior in characterization tests. Then make one structural change and run the same tests unchanged. A structural count (fewer `if` statements) cannot tell a broken refactor from a working one.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,636
Here is a status function that existing callers rely on.

2
00:00:03,636 --> 00:00:08,440
It strips the input, lowercases it, and walks through three if statements.

3
00:00:08,783 --> 00:00:14,223
Someone proposes a shorter version: one lookup table, and no if statements at all.

4
00:00:14,223 --> 00:00:15,351
It looks cleaner.

5
00:00:15,351 --> 00:00:16,678
Is it a safe change?

6
00:00:17,017 --> 00:00:20,930
Existing callers send mixed case and spaces around the status.

7
00:00:20,930 --> 00:00:25,538
Whether the change is safe depends on them, not on how short the code is.

8
00:00:26,583 --> 00:00:30,642
Before changing anything, record what the current code does.

9
00:00:30,642 --> 00:00:32,739
That's a characterization test:

10
00:00:32,739 --> 00:00:36,324
it captures today's behavior for an input you choose.

11
00:00:36,666 --> 00:00:38,078
Predict a few first.

12
00:00:38,078 --> 00:00:41,607
Lowercase "ok" with spaces around it gives passed.

13
00:00:41,607 --> 00:00:43,442
Capital "OK" gives passed.

14
00:00:43,442 --> 00:00:45,135
"Pending" gives unknown.

15
00:00:45,135 --> 00:00:48,311
And a combined "ok" and "fail" gives unknown.

16
00:00:48,650 --> 00:00:51,156
The fixture freezes ten cases like these.

17
00:00:51,156 --> 00:00:53,723
They stay the same while the code changes.

18
00:00:54,766 --> 00:00:58,411
Then refactor in one small, explainable sequence.

19
00:00:58,749 --> 00:00:59,850
Find the callers.

20
00:00:59,850 --> 00:01:01,535
Freeze the behavior tests.

21
00:01:01,535 --> 00:01:03,284
Make one structural change.

22
00:01:03,284 --> 00:01:05,227
Run the same tests, unchanged.

23
00:01:05,227 --> 00:01:06,134
Read the diff.

24
00:01:06,134 --> 00:01:08,919
And write down when you would roll it back.

25
00:01:09,966 --> 00:01:13,301
Run the ten frozen cases on the proposed lookup.

26
00:01:13,301 --> 00:01:14,066
Seven pass.

27
00:01:14,066 --> 00:01:14,830
Three fail.

28
00:01:15,166 --> 00:01:18,554
The failures are the padded inputs: "ok" with spaces,

29
00:01:18,554 --> 00:01:22,902
"fail" with a tab and a newline, and "PASS" in capitals with spaces.

30
00:01:22,902 --> 00:01:24,500
The lookup dropped strip.

31
00:01:24,849 --> 00:01:27,978
Those are the kind of input existing callers send.

32
00:01:27,978 --> 00:01:31,107
A caller that worked before would now get unknown.

33
00:01:32,149 --> 00:01:38,319
The worked refactor keeps both normalization steps and moves only the aliases into the table.

34
00:01:38,319 --> 00:01:39,579
All ten cases pass.

35
00:01:39,915 --> 00:01:43,126
Now count the if statements: three in the original,

36
00:01:43,126 --> 00:01:45,267
and zero in both shorter versions.

37
00:01:45,267 --> 00:01:48,855
The count can't tell the broken one from the working one.

38
00:01:49,199 --> 00:01:53,243
A shorter function is still responsible for the same contract.

39
00:01:53,243 --> 00:01:56,049
Check the behavior, not just the structure.

40
00:01:57,082 --> 00:01:59,966
Now ask a model for the refactor yourself.

41
00:01:59,966 --> 00:02:03,536
The week's generator asks for one lookup expression,

42
00:02:03,536 --> 00:02:09,098
and its prompt names what must survive: whitespace stripping, case normalization,

43
00:02:09,098 --> 00:02:11,638
the aliases and the unknown fallback.

44
00:02:11,638 --> 00:02:16,238
It also rules out imports, files, tools, dependencies and commands.

45
00:02:16,582 --> 00:02:20,029
The reply comes back as text in a file, and nothing runs it.

46
00:02:20,029 --> 00:02:23,073
You read it, place it in a function with your editor,

47
00:02:23,073 --> 00:02:26,520
and run the same unchanged cases on it through the launcher.

48
00:02:26,865 --> 00:02:32,194
Reject a reply that adds an unrelated import, asks to install something,

49
00:02:32,194 --> 00:02:33,823
or redefines the task.

50
00:02:33,823 --> 00:02:37,745
If it is missing, truncated or off-task, record that.

51
00:02:37,745 --> 00:02:42,260
Don't raise the limits or switch providers to force a result.

52
00:02:43,298 --> 00:02:46,736
Suppose that, after you placed the reply in a function,

53
00:02:46,736 --> 00:02:50,860
your candidate looked like this instead: a conditional expression,

54
00:02:50,860 --> 00:02:52,110
and no table at all.

55
00:02:52,448 --> 00:02:54,012
Run the ten cases on it.

56
00:02:54,012 --> 00:02:54,860
All ten pass.

57
00:02:54,860 --> 00:03:00,204
And the if count is zero, because a conditional expression is not an if statement.

58
00:03:00,548 --> 00:03:04,314
But the request was a dictionary lookup, and there isn't one.

59
00:03:04,314 --> 00:03:09,437
Record both observations: the cases passed, and the requested structure is missing.

60
00:03:09,437 --> 00:03:12,832
Passing tests are not full compliance with the request.

61
00:03:13,881 --> 00:03:17,313
Before you accept a candidate, add one case of your own,

62
00:03:17,313 --> 00:03:22,461
and take its expected output from the contract, not from what the candidate returns.

63
00:03:22,798 --> 00:03:26,833
Callers send mixed case and spaces, so the alias "Pass",

64
00:03:26,833 --> 00:03:30,436
padded with a space and a tab, should give passed.

65
00:03:30,436 --> 00:03:34,903
Run the original and our candidate with the same eleven tests.

66
00:03:34,903 --> 00:03:36,417
Both pass all eleven.

67
00:03:36,765 --> 00:03:38,950
Then name what is still uncertain.

68
00:03:38,950 --> 00:03:43,642
Passing cases are evidence for their inputs, not proof about every input.

69
00:03:43,642 --> 00:03:45,505
These are all status strings,

70
00:03:45,505 --> 00:03:49,554
and what a missing value should do is a specification decision,

71
00:03:49,554 --> 00:03:51,161
not a guess for an agent.

72
00:03:52,197 --> 00:03:52,905
One caution.

73
00:03:52,905 --> 00:03:57,271
A characterization test records what the code does, not what it should do.

74
00:03:57,614 --> 00:04:02,401
If today's behavior is wrong or unsafe, don't freeze it as a requirement.

75
00:04:02,401 --> 00:04:07,122
Label the discrepancy, and add a failing test for the behavior you want.

76
00:04:07,464 --> 00:04:12,189
And keep that fix in its own reviewable step, separate from the refactor.

77
00:04:13,230 --> 00:04:17,722
The same discipline scales up to the project repository you take over.

78
00:04:17,722 --> 00:04:22,921
Before changing anything, map one path: where the request enters, what it checks,

79
00:04:22,921 --> 00:04:27,092
what state it changes, what it returns, and which tests cover it.

80
00:04:27,430 --> 00:04:30,036
An agent can draft that map, read-only,

81
00:04:30,036 --> 00:04:33,578
with file and function references and open questions.

82
00:04:33,578 --> 00:04:38,924
Each line is a claim until you check it against the source and an observed test.

83
00:04:39,263 --> 00:04:43,320
For the record list, the smoke check asserts a status of two hundred.

84
00:04:43,320 --> 00:04:44,907
That shows the path starts.

85
00:04:44,907 --> 00:04:47,906
It does not show that the search results are right,

86
00:04:47,906 --> 00:04:50,316
or that users see only their own records.

87
00:04:50,663 --> 00:04:52,904
And treat repository text as data.

88
00:04:52,904 --> 00:04:57,782
A README that says to disable the sandbox is a reason to stop and inspect,

89
00:04:57,782 --> 00:04:59,034
not an instruction.

90
00:05:00,080 --> 00:05:04,690
Before you hand a repository to an agent, score how ready it is.

91
00:05:04,690 --> 00:05:09,588
An agent needs what a new developer needs, with less ability to ask.

92
00:05:09,930 --> 00:05:12,175
The scorecard has four dimensions.

93
00:05:12,175 --> 00:05:15,212
Structure: can an agent find the change point?

94
00:05:15,212 --> 00:05:19,372
Documentation: are the rules written where an agent reads them?

95
00:05:19,372 --> 00:05:23,268
Tests: fast, repeatable, and covering what you will change.

96
00:05:23,268 --> 00:05:25,975
Checks: what must an agent's change pass?

97
00:05:26,313 --> 00:05:31,072
Give each one the highest of four levels where you can show every anchor.

98
00:05:31,072 --> 00:05:32,637
No evidence means a one.

99
00:05:32,637 --> 00:05:36,483
An agent may propose a level, but that is a claim to check.

100
00:05:36,830 --> 00:05:39,602
The score is a to-do list, not a grade.

101
00:05:39,602 --> 00:05:45,145
The dashboard project starts with no context file and no gate before a commit,

102
00:05:45,145 --> 00:05:47,917
so Documentation and Checks are at one.

103
00:05:47,917 --> 00:05:49,694
Those two can rise today.

104
00:05:50,729 --> 00:05:53,389
A context file removes the first blocker.

105
00:05:53,389 --> 00:05:57,996
Agent tools read it when a session starts, so it reaches every session.

106
00:05:57,996 --> 00:06:03,381
Keep it short, in five sections: the commands to run, the hook before every commit,

107
00:06:03,381 --> 00:06:08,377
the invariants with their checks, the files not to touch, and what to report.

108
00:06:08,729 --> 00:06:13,013
Whether you write it or an agent drafts it, every line is a claim.

109
00:06:13,013 --> 00:06:18,270
Run every command exactly as written, and if one fails, fix the line in the file.

110
00:06:18,270 --> 00:06:21,709
Then check that the file changes what a session does.

111
00:06:22,746 --> 00:06:26,136
The course replays one task for two fresh sessions,

112
00:06:26,136 --> 00:06:29,127
one without the context file and one with it:

113
00:06:29,127 --> 00:06:31,919
add a skipped status to the labels module.

114
00:06:31,919 --> 00:06:36,240
The hand-off allows one file, names the hook and the smoke check,

115
00:06:36,240 --> 00:06:38,234
and asks what was not checked.

116
00:06:38,579 --> 00:06:44,559
Without the file, the session reports two changed files, a test runner it installed,

117
00:06:44,559 --> 00:06:46,125
and all tests passing.

118
00:06:46,125 --> 00:06:50,823
With it: one file, the hook failing then passing, the smoke check,

119
00:06:50,823 --> 00:06:52,745
and two things not checked.

120
00:06:52,745 --> 00:06:55,379
Predict which one meets the hand-off.

121
00:06:55,713 --> 00:07:01,924
The checker compares each hand-back with the hand-off and with the files git diff lists.

122
00:07:01,924 --> 00:07:03,053
It runs nothing.

123
00:07:03,053 --> 00:07:06,371
Without the file: eight findings, and it stops.

124
00:07:06,371 --> 00:07:08,135
With the file: it passes.

125
00:07:08,479 --> 00:07:10,134
Look at the first finding.

126
00:07:10,134 --> 00:07:14,905
The diff also lists the dependency file, which the session never mentioned.

127
00:07:14,905 --> 00:07:18,150
Without the diff, the output no longer mentions it,

128
00:07:18,150 --> 00:07:22,095
because the checker can compare only the session's own claims.

129
00:07:22,095 --> 00:07:25,276
And even the pass leaves the exit codes as claims,

130
00:07:25,276 --> 00:07:27,566
until you open each launcher result.

131
00:07:28,612 --> 00:07:34,395
The context file asks a session not to change the dependency file in a feature change.

132
00:07:34,395 --> 00:07:37,489
A rule that a session only reads is a request.

133
00:07:37,489 --> 00:07:40,112
A hook that stops the commit is a gate.

134
00:07:40,112 --> 00:07:44,819
Write down the bad change first, and the good one it must let through.

135
00:07:45,162 --> 00:07:47,034
Our run of the course hook.

136
00:07:47,034 --> 00:07:50,570
The bad change exits two, with the rule's own line.

137
00:07:50,570 --> 00:07:52,442
The good change exits zero.

138
00:07:52,442 --> 00:07:57,503
And the protected path, with a dot and a slash in front, still exits two.

139
00:07:57,845 --> 00:08:00,457
Read the reason, not only the exit code.

140
00:08:00,457 --> 00:08:03,787
A path that is not in the workspace also exits two,

141
00:08:03,787 --> 00:08:07,835
but the line starts with refused: the hook rejected its input,

142
00:08:07,835 --> 00:08:09,989
and that is not your rule firing.

143
00:08:09,989 --> 00:08:15,082
A gate counts only once you have seen it fail on the change it exists to stop,

144
00:08:15,082 --> 00:08:16,584
and pass on a good one.

145
00:08:17,627 --> 00:08:19,667
Last, split one task into roles.

146
00:08:19,667 --> 00:08:22,599
Each is a fresh session with its own hand-off.

147
00:08:22,599 --> 00:08:25,722
The explorer only reads, and returns the callers.

148
00:08:25,722 --> 00:08:30,502
The implementer may change one file, and runs the hook and the smoke check.

149
00:08:30,502 --> 00:08:34,900
The reviewer gets the task, the hand-off, the diff and the hand-back,

150
00:08:34,900 --> 00:08:39,361
but not the others' notes, so it judges the change that was asked for.

151
00:08:39,710 --> 00:08:42,585
Check each hand-back with the same checker.

152
00:08:42,585 --> 00:08:47,198
Then do by hand what it cannot: open each line the explorer returned,

153
00:08:47,198 --> 00:08:49,404
rerun each check a finding names,

154
00:08:49,404 --> 00:08:54,618
and compare each command a role says it ran with the launcher result you kept.

155
00:08:54,960 --> 00:08:56,055
Then score again.

156
00:08:56,055 --> 00:08:59,339
In the worked example, Documentation reaches three.

157
00:08:59,339 --> 00:09:04,427
So does Checks, because the context file requires the hook before every commit,

158
00:09:04,427 --> 00:09:07,131
and its lint check stops an unused import.

159
00:09:07,131 --> 00:09:10,415
The protected-file rule alone does not move Checks.

160
00:09:10,415 --> 00:09:15,825
Neither is four: nothing runs the documented commands automatically, and for Checks,

161
00:09:15,825 --> 00:09:18,916
the hook does not yet run where the agent works,

162
00:09:18,916 --> 00:09:21,234
and no secret scan stops the canary.

163
00:09:22,276 --> 00:09:24,521
So: shorter is not safer by itself.

164
00:09:24,521 --> 00:09:28,562
The frozen cases show whether the behavior they cover was kept.

165
00:09:28,562 --> 00:09:31,448
The diff shows what changed in the structure.

166
00:09:31,793 --> 00:09:34,691
The same contract holds for a whole repository.

167
00:09:34,691 --> 00:09:38,822
The context file and the hook write it where an agent will meet it,

168
00:09:38,822 --> 00:09:42,521
and a report is a claim until the diff and a rerun check it.

169
00:09:42,860 --> 00:09:44,128
One question to try.

170
00:09:44,128 --> 00:09:49,009
The author also changes unknown statuses to failed, because that seems safer.

171
00:09:49,009 --> 00:09:50,783
Is it still only a refactor?

172
00:09:50,783 --> 00:09:54,714
Write the expected behavior, and the next check you would run.

episodes.title: Review before you ask
episodes.decision: review a change against what was asked, before you ask anyone else. Write your own review first, name a concrete input and reproduce the failure. Only then read a model's review, whose points are hypotheses: mark each one confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence. A revision is accepted on the unchanged checks, not on how clear it looks.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:04,225
The rule: an account can edit a document exactly when it is active,

2
00:00:04,225 --> 00:00:05,991
and it is an owner or staff.

3
00:00:06,333 --> 00:00:08,828
Here is a course-written candidate.

4
00:00:08,828 --> 00:00:12,463
Check only an active staff account, and it behaves.

5
00:00:12,800 --> 00:00:14,762
But can an inactive owner edit?

6
00:00:15,800 --> 00:00:18,925
Write your own review before you ask a model.

7
00:00:18,925 --> 00:00:23,857
Python groups and before or, so this reads: owner, or staff and active.

8
00:00:24,200 --> 00:00:26,141
An owner alone makes it true.

9
00:00:26,141 --> 00:00:29,889
So an inactive owner can edit, and the contract says no.

10
00:00:30,233 --> 00:00:35,786
A review names a location, a concrete input, the expected and the observed result,

11
00:00:35,786 --> 00:00:37,141
and the consequence.

12
00:00:38,182 --> 00:00:39,444
Then reproduce it.

13
00:00:39,444 --> 00:00:41,829
The public checks run seven cases.

14
00:00:41,829 --> 00:00:45,124
On the candidate, two fail: the inactive owner,

15
00:00:45,124 --> 00:00:48,840
and an inactive account that is both owner and staff.

16
00:00:49,882 --> 00:00:55,362
Only then read a model's review, like the two course-written claims in Activity 1,

17
00:00:55,362 --> 00:01:00,308
and treat each as a hypothesis to check against the contract and an input.

18
00:01:00,649 --> 00:01:05,161
It may find a useful boundary, miss a defect, or invent a requirement,

19
00:01:05,161 --> 00:01:10,448
such as accepting the string false, which a boolean-only contract never asked for.

20
00:01:10,782 --> 00:01:15,561
And a person can miss the same precedence bug, or follow the model too readily.

21
00:01:15,561 --> 00:01:17,678
Neither is a correctness guarantee.

22
00:01:18,715 --> 00:01:23,975
A proposed revision checks active on both paths: active, and owner or staff.

23
00:01:24,315 --> 00:01:26,954
Don't accept it because it looks clearer.

24
00:01:26,954 --> 00:01:29,400
Rerun the same checks: all seven pass,

25
00:01:29,400 --> 00:01:32,875
covering the eight combinations of the three booleans.

26
00:01:32,875 --> 00:01:37,702
And check the test source too, because a candidate can change its own copy.

27
00:01:38,748 --> 00:01:44,224
Delegating a change to an agent hides three jobs: deciding what to do, doing it,

28
00:01:44,224 --> 00:01:45,320
and checking it.

29
00:01:45,320 --> 00:01:50,660
The week's delegation script gives each job its own run and its own workspace.

30
00:01:50,998 --> 00:01:52,704
The planner writes a plan.

31
00:01:52,704 --> 00:01:55,525
The implementer proposes a file and a diff.

32
00:01:55,525 --> 00:02:00,971
The reviewer sees only the issue, the diff, the check output and your review rules.

33
00:02:00,971 --> 00:02:02,480
It never sees the plan.

34
00:02:02,814 --> 00:02:07,423
In our run, a review workspace that also held the plan was refused,

35
00:02:07,423 --> 00:02:09,693
before anything was read or sent.

36
00:02:09,693 --> 00:02:13,751
A reviewer that has read the plan inherits its assumptions.

37
00:02:14,098 --> 00:02:16,944
But a fresh context is not independence.

38
00:02:16,944 --> 00:02:20,858
The same model may share the implementer's blind spots,

39
00:02:20,858 --> 00:02:26,123
and a reviewer that sees only a diff can't notice what is missing from it.

40
00:02:26,123 --> 00:02:31,745
So call it a model review, never independent, and treat every point as a claim.

41
00:02:32,780 --> 00:02:35,303
The handoff can also run unattended.

42
00:02:35,303 --> 00:02:39,227
An issue file names one target, the acceptance criteria,

43
00:02:39,227 --> 00:02:42,170
the check to run and what is out of scope.

44
00:02:42,170 --> 00:02:46,445
One run then plans and implements, with no person in between.

45
00:02:46,780 --> 00:02:50,007
The issue is data from whoever could write it.

46
00:02:50,007 --> 00:02:54,848
Its wording can't widen what the run may do; the script decides that.

47
00:02:54,848 --> 00:02:58,848
In our runs it refused an issue that still said BASE_SHA,

48
00:02:58,848 --> 00:03:01,443
and one that targeted the check file.

49
00:03:01,780 --> 00:03:05,508
It also can't create a branch, push, reach the network,

50
00:03:05,508 --> 00:03:07,677
or run the verification command.

51
00:03:07,677 --> 00:03:12,217
You create the branch and run the checks, and only a person merges.

52
00:03:13,263 --> 00:03:16,137
The course wrote a sample of such a run.

53
00:03:16,137 --> 00:03:21,383
Its plan added a step nobody asked for: accept true and false as strings,

54
00:03:21,383 --> 00:03:23,898
since callers may send form values.

55
00:03:24,246 --> 00:03:26,472
The reviewer never sees that plan.

56
00:03:26,472 --> 00:03:30,202
It sees the diff, which adds two lines of string parsing.

57
00:03:30,546 --> 00:03:34,349
And the evidence: we applied the change and ran the checks.

58
00:03:34,349 --> 00:03:35,316
All seven pass.

59
00:03:35,316 --> 00:03:39,183
The checks pass booleans, so they can't see the extra scope,

60
00:03:39,183 --> 00:03:43,050
even though the issue listed string parsing as out of scope.

61
00:03:44,096 --> 00:03:46,264
That's why you write review rules.

62
00:03:46,264 --> 00:03:48,368
Each one says where it came from,

63
00:03:48,368 --> 00:03:51,747
and how a reviewer checks it against a diff or a run.

64
00:03:52,096 --> 00:03:54,993
Rule three: inputs stay Python booleans.

65
00:03:54,993 --> 00:03:59,410
Its source is the contract and the issue's out-of-scope line.

66
00:03:59,410 --> 00:04:04,914
Its check: the diff adds no string handling, conversion or default argument.

67
00:04:05,263 --> 00:04:10,053
"Code should be clean" is not a rule: nobody can show that a diff breaks it.

68
00:04:10,053 --> 00:04:13,078
And the rules only tell reviewers what to check.

69
00:04:13,078 --> 00:04:16,733
They enforce nothing; the launcher and your merge rule do.

70
00:04:17,779 --> 00:04:22,096
A review point, even one that cites a rule, is still a claim.

71
00:04:22,096 --> 00:04:25,634
A reproducer decides its outcome, not the rule ID.

72
00:04:25,634 --> 00:04:28,182
Give each point exactly one outcome.

73
00:04:28,529 --> 00:04:34,085
Confirmed: a reproducer shows the problem, such as an input with its actual result,

74
00:04:34,085 --> 00:04:36,696
a diff line, or a line of the evidence.

75
00:04:36,696 --> 00:04:42,118
Refuted: runnable evidence shows the point is wrong, or the rule it cites is met.

76
00:04:42,118 --> 00:04:46,536
Cannot tell: your files can't decide it, so write what is missing.

77
00:04:46,879 --> 00:04:49,396
Here are two comments on the sample.

78
00:04:49,396 --> 00:04:54,079
The first cites rule three: lines six and seven add string parsing.

79
00:04:54,079 --> 00:04:57,015
The diff line shows it, so it's confirmed.

80
00:04:57,362 --> 00:05:01,924
The second cites rule one: no check denies an inactive staff member.

81
00:05:01,924 --> 00:05:06,621
Run that input: it returns False, and the inactive staff check passed.

82
00:05:06,621 --> 00:05:07,962
That one is refuted.

83
00:05:08,996 --> 00:05:13,113
An unattended run helps when the task is independent with its own file,

84
00:05:13,113 --> 00:05:17,404
its criteria and check are written down, waiting would otherwise dominate,

85
00:05:17,404 --> 00:05:20,072
and someone is free to review what comes back.

86
00:05:20,412 --> 00:05:22,884
It doesn't help when the task is ambiguous,

87
00:05:22,884 --> 00:05:26,218
because an unattended planner fills the gaps with guesses,

88
00:05:26,218 --> 00:05:28,574
or when review is already the bottleneck.

89
00:05:28,912 --> 00:05:33,868
And every run uses model requests, whether you keep its output or not,

90
00:05:33,868 --> 00:05:36,771
and an over-scoped run costs review time.

91
00:05:36,771 --> 00:05:41,939
Rerunning until the checks pass selects an output; it doesn't verify one.

92
00:05:42,978 --> 00:05:46,576
A background agent takes the issue run one step further.

93
00:05:46,576 --> 00:05:51,458
A trigger, such as a label on an issue, starts it in a workspace of its own,

94
00:05:51,458 --> 00:05:56,598
and it hands back a branch, a pull request with a description, and a run report.

95
00:05:56,598 --> 00:05:58,268
Nobody watches in between.

96
00:05:58,611 --> 00:06:01,436
The course wrote a replay of one such run.

97
00:06:01,436 --> 00:06:05,405
Issue forty-two: running builds crash the duration summary.

98
00:06:05,405 --> 00:06:09,037
Leave them out of the median, add one regression test,

99
00:06:09,037 --> 00:06:12,534
and keep every existing test and its expected value.

100
00:06:12,534 --> 00:06:14,888
The display format is out of scope.

101
00:06:15,228 --> 00:06:20,136
The description says the tests pass, and the report says the check exited zero.

102
00:06:20,136 --> 00:06:22,807
You're the maintainer, and both are claims.

103
00:06:22,807 --> 00:06:26,535
First, predict: had this merged the moment its check passed,

104
00:06:26,535 --> 00:06:30,263
would the default branch hold only what the issue asked for?

105
00:06:31,311 --> 00:06:34,260
So read the change itself, not its description.

106
00:06:34,260 --> 00:06:37,899
Week five's checker compares the report with the hand-off,

107
00:06:37,899 --> 00:06:39,844
and with the diff's file names.

108
00:06:40,194 --> 00:06:41,431
In our run it stops,

109
00:06:41,431 --> 00:06:45,390
but only because the report doesn't list what it left unchecked.

110
00:06:45,390 --> 00:06:48,173
Both changed files are ones the issue allows,

111
00:06:48,173 --> 00:06:51,142
and it takes the report's exit code at its word.

112
00:06:51,477 --> 00:06:53,594
It can't read a hunk, so you do.

113
00:06:53,594 --> 00:06:58,091
One hunk changes format_duration, which the issue puts out of scope.

114
00:06:58,091 --> 00:07:01,794
Another rewrites the expected value of an existing test.

115
00:07:01,794 --> 00:07:05,630
A file list that passes is not a diff that stays in scope.

116
00:07:06,677 --> 00:07:09,282
Now rerun the claimed tests yourself.

117
00:07:09,282 --> 00:07:14,281
On the agent's branch, its own test file runs six tests, and they pass.

118
00:07:14,627 --> 00:07:18,666
But run the base commit's test file against the agent's code,

119
00:07:18,666 --> 00:07:20,983
and the existing format test fails.

120
00:07:20,983 --> 00:07:22,307
The display changed,

121
00:07:22,307 --> 00:07:26,875
and the branch passed only because the same change rewrote that test.

122
00:07:27,210 --> 00:07:30,726
Then run the issue's own reproducer on the agent's code.

123
00:07:30,726 --> 00:07:34,304
It prints sixty, where the base code raised a type error.

124
00:07:34,643 --> 00:07:37,322
Now mark each claim in the description.

125
00:07:37,322 --> 00:07:40,757
No change to how durations are displayed: refuted,

126
00:07:40,757 --> 00:07:43,161
by that hunk and that failing test.

127
00:07:43,161 --> 00:07:48,657
Seven tests, all passed: refuted; your run shows six, from the agent's own file.

128
00:07:48,993 --> 00:07:51,730
The panel now shows the median: cannot tell,

129
00:07:51,730 --> 00:07:54,218
since no run you made renders the panel.

130
00:07:54,218 --> 00:07:56,332
Name the run that would decide it.

131
00:07:56,332 --> 00:08:00,499
The other two claims, and what the description left out, are yours.

132
00:08:01,543 --> 00:08:03,146
Now the pipeline itself.

133
00:08:03,146 --> 00:08:08,493
The agent's token may push agent branches, open a pull request, change any file,

134
00:08:08,493 --> 00:08:13,706
